pathophysiology.summary: Cancer pain arises from tumour invasion of bone, viscera, nerves and soft tissue, from treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy) and from unrelated causes. Most patients have mixed nociceptive and neuropathic pain, and pain often has background and breakthrough components.
keyMechanisms: Nociceptive somatic pain (bone, soft tissue) is well localised; visceral pain (liver capsule, bowel) is poorly localised and may be colicky.

Neuropathic pain from nerve compression or infiltration is burning, tingling or shooting and responds partially to opioids — adjuvants such as amitriptyline or gabapentin are needed (MOH Protocol-010).
Tumour-related oedema and inflammation (nerve compression, liver capsule stretch, raised intracranial pressure) respond to corticosteroids.
Opioids act on mu receptors; side effects (constipation in nearly all, transient nausea, sedation, respiratory depression) are predictable (NICE CG140).

symptoms: Pain site, character, intensity (0–10), timing, background versus breakthrough, response to previous analgesics.
Burning or shooting pain, numbness (neuropathic); colic (bowel); headache with vomiting (raised intracranial pressure).
Impact on sleep, mood, mobility; fears about opioids (addiction, tolerance, 'final stage').
physicalSigns: Bone tenderness, pathological fracture; neurological deficit (cord or root compression).
Hepatomegaly; bowel distension; signs of opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, myoclonus, drowsiness).
Behavioural pain signs if communication is limited (grimacing, guarding, restlessness).
redFlags: New back pain with leg weakness, sensory level or sphincter change — spinal cord compression: dexamethasone 16 mg daily and urgent oncology/radiotherapy
Pain 7–10/10 uncontrolled after titration (severe pain band)
Opioid toxicity: drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, respiratory depression
Pathological fracture; signs of bowel obstruction or perforation
precipitants: Bone metastases, nerve infiltration, visceral involvement
Inadequate background dosing or poor adherence

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Back pain with neurological signs; needs urgent MRI and steroids.
Sudden severe localised bone pain, deformity.
Worsening pain with escalating dose, allodynia, myoclonus.
Reversible cause; NICE NG31 lists urinary retention.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Score pain 0–10 and classify mild (1–3), moderate (4–6) or severe (7–10); identify neuropathic, bone and visceral components.
Give analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation (MOH Protocol-003).
Ask about fears of addiction and side effects; give written information on background and breakthrough dosing (NICE CG140).

clinicalManagement.title: Mild pain (1–3/10)
actions: Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg PO every 4–6 h, maximum 4,000 mg/day — avoid in liver dysfunction (MOH Protocol-010 p. 7).
Or an NSAID (one only) if no renal dysfunction, GI bleeding or coagulopathy: ibuprofen 400–800 mg PO every 6–8 h, maximum 3,200 mg/day.
Or a weak opioid: codeine 30–60 mg PO every 4 h (maximum 400 mg/day, MOH Protocol-003) or tramadol 50–100 mg every 4–6 h (maximum 400 mg/day).

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate–severe pain (5 or more/10)
actions: Morphine is first line (MOH, NICE). MOH Protocol-003: morphine 5 mg PO every 4 h regularly plus 2.5–5 mg every 1 h PRN.
NICE CG140 (no renal/hepatic disease): 20–30 mg oral morphine per day, e.g. 10–15 mg sustained-release twice daily, plus 5 mg immediate-release for breakthrough.
Alternatives: oxycodone 5 mg PO every 4 h plus 5 mg every 1 h PRN; hydromorphone 1 mg every 4 h plus 0.5–1 mg PRN (MOH Protocol-003).
Prescribe a regular laxative for everyone starting a strong opioid (NICE CG140).

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate
actions: More than 3 PRN doses a day: raise the total daily dose by 25–75%, or add the 24-h PRN total to the regular total and divide by 6 for the 4-hourly dose (MOH Protocol-003).
Switch opioid if pain is uncontrolled despite titration or toxicity occurs; optimise laxatives before switching for constipation (NICE).
Use transdermal patches only when oral opioids are unsuitable and requirements are stable; no fast-acting fentanyl as first-line rescue (NICE CG140).
Patch to oral: remove patch 6 h before the first oral modified-release dose and give half the equivalent dose for the first 24 h (MOH Protocol-010 p. 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Neuropathic and adjuvant analgesia
actions: Neuropathic pain: step 1 gabapentin/pregabalin or amitriptyline; step 2 combine; step 3 specialist palliative care advice (MOH Protocol-010 p. 5).
Corticosteroid adjuvant: dexamethasone 8–16 mg daily for liver capsule pain or nerve compression; give before noon; review within 7 days (MOH Protocol-010 p. 4).
Spinal cord compression: dexamethasone 16 mg daily for 5 days, 8 mg during radiotherapy, then reduce over 2 weeks (MOH Protocol-010 p. 4).
Co-prescribe a PPI when combining NSAIDs, steroids, SSRIs or anticoagulants (MOH Protocol-010).

patientEducation: Background versus breakthrough doses; safe storage of opioids.
Constipation is expected — take laxatives regularly.
Nausea at the start is usually transient (NICE).
lifestyleAndDiet: Activity pacing; heat, positioning, TENS where helpful (MOH).
mdtReferrals: Oncology/radiotherapy for bone pain or cord compression.
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms controlled for the chosen place of care, or safe transfer arranged.
Patient and family know the plan, the medicines and whom to call.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review frequently during titration (NICE CG140), at least daily as an inpatient; specialist palliative care referral if pain is not controlled after a few dose adjustments or adverse effects persist.
